benchmarks.note: independent mechanic-written guide: replacing one lower or upper arm costs $160 to $390, with a wheel alignment adding $60 to $120; no vehicle named and no date on the figures

finding: The live range of $240-$1,200 is about right. It is wide, but the evidence is that wide: the arm itself runs from about $65 (aftermarket, economy car) to about $610 (Ford list price for a truck lower arm), and the published benchmarks alone span $160 to over $1,200. Built totals for one front lower arm, parts + stated hours x $120-$160/hr (the national middle labor rate used for these checks), with no alignment: economy 2015 Corolla about $149-$470 (0.7-1.5 hr); midsize 2016 CR-V about $187-$776 (0.6-1.5 hr); truck 2016 F-150 about $469-$1,089 (2.0-3.0 hr); luxury 2015 BMW 328i about $198-$566 (1.0-2.0 hr). The bottom: our lowest totals ($149-$198) pair an online aftermarket price with a manufacturer warranty time and leave out the wheel alignment that almost always follows this job; the manufacturer bulletins allow 0.4-0.7 hr for it, which is roughly $50-$110 more, so $240 is a fair floor for a real quote and the lowest benchmark ($160-$390 plus $60-$120 alignment) agrees. The top: a truck arm at list plus 3 hours is about $1,089, and RepairPal shows $1,176-$1,222 for a 2015 BMW 328i xDrive, so $1,200 fits. Our mainstream totals sit below RepairPal's $791-$909 average mainly because of parts: RepairPal assumes $571-$587 in parts, close to dealer list, while a good aftermarket arm for the same cars is $65-$230. How solid the labor times are: economy is a GM warranty time for a Chevrolet Trax (0.7 hr), not a Corolla; midsize is a Honda warranty time for a 2006 CR-V (0.6 hr), the same model but an older design, backed by a 2021 Jeep Cherokee warranty time (1.4 hr), and a 2018 Jeep Compass bulletin allows 2.4 hr, so some crossovers will run above our range; truck uses a parts seller's 2-hour and 3-hour figures for the F-150 itself, not a book time; luxury is the weakest, a DIY guide's 1-2 hours for the F30 that covers a full set of front arms on all-wheel-drive cars. The upper ends for economy and midsize rest on a general statement of 1-1.5 hours per arm. Warranty times are the low end of what shops bill, and rusted or seized bolts add time.
extras: A quote almost always adds a wheel alignment (manufacturer bulletins allow 0.4-0.7 hr for it; one guide puts it at $60-$120). Shops often recommend doing the other side at the same time, which roughly doubles parts and adds less than double the labor. Also common: new sway bar (stabilizer) links if their nuts are seized, new one-time-use bolts and nuts, a separate ball joint or bushings if the arm is not sold with them, a second arm on the same side on cars that have two (the BMW tension strut), extra labor for rusted or seized bolts, a suspension inspection or diagnosis fee, shop supplies and sales tax.
